Odile’s voice

September 2037, in Odile’s flat on rue d’Austerlitz. Isabelle, who was an editor for thirty years, has gathered her mother’s notebooks, the letters and the twenty-three logbooks of her father, Henri. She wants to turn them into a book. Hortense Valmont and Julien have come to read the manuscript.
Here is the manuscript I told you about: my mother’s notebooks, my father’s letters and his twenty-three logbooks.
It’s magnificent. But some sentences will have to be rewritten. The style is sometimes too informal.
Too informal? It’s Odile’s voice, the one she spoke to us with every day.
Julien is right. A book in which you correct everything has no soul left.
I’m not talking about correcting everything. I’m talking about the preface, which will be read by thousands of people.
Then write it yourself. Your formal style is exactly what the preface needs.
Gladly. I’ll begin like this: “Posthumous publication of the notebooks of Odile Bernard, doctor, neighbour and guardian of silence.”
(she laughs) You can tell she’s a journalist. A sentence with no verb, like a newspaper headline.
And the title of the book? It has to be chosen before the end of the month, the printer is waiting for it.
I thought of the sentence from her letter, the one you’re so attached to: “Leave your door open”.
It’s simple, it’s everyday language, and it’s understood in every language. It’s perfect.
What I like is that she would have said exactly that. No capital letter, no exclamation mark.
Then it’s decided. The book will be published on 3 May next year, the day of the lime trees.

“Ma-noo-skree”: “u” = the French “u”, silent final “t”.
“Luh-kel”: “qu” = “k”, weak “e” in the first syllable.
“Pos-toom”: “th” = “t”, “u” = the French “u”.
“Pray-fass”: “c” before “e” = “s”.
“Day-no-mee-na-syohn”: “-tion” = “syohn”.
1. Nominalisation: from verb to noun
In headlines, notes, official texts and journalism, French turns clauses into noun phrases. The sentence becomes shorter and “colder”:
Verbal clause
Le livre sera publié en mai.
Publication du livre en mai.
La mairie a décidé de nommer le jardin.
Décision de la mairie de nommer le jardin.
Les carnets ont été découverts en 2031.
Découverte des carnets en 2031.
On a ouvert la médiathèque.
Ouverture de la médiathèque.
Augmentation des prix.

The most common suffixes: -tion (publier → la publication), -ment (lancer → le lancement), -age (nettoyer → le nettoyage), -ure (ouvrir → l’ouverture), -ée (arriver → l’arrivée), -ance (naître → la naissance).

Watch the gender of the nouns: “le lancement” (masculine, like all nouns in -ment), but “la publication” (feminine, like all nouns in -tion). And watch the complement: after a noun comes “de” — “la construction DU pont”, not “la construction le pont” ✗.
2. The passive and its alternatives
Passive = “être” in the required tense + past participle, which agrees with the subject. The agent is introduced with “par” (sometimes with “de” after verbs of feeling or state).
The preface will be read by thousands of people. (future)
The notebooks were found in a trunk. (passé composé)
Odile was loved by the whole neighbourhood. (feeling → “de”)
Spoken French uses the passive less often than written English. The alternatives:
Alternative
on + active
On a retrouvé les carnets.
pronominal verb with a passive meaning
Ça se comprend dans toutes les langues.
se faire + infinitive (the person undergoes the action)
Il s’est fait corriger par Hortense.
Not every verb has a passive: verbs with no direct object (“obéir à”, “téléphoner à”) cannot be put into the passive. “Il a été téléphoné” ✗ → “On lui a téléphoné” ✓.
3. Relative pronouns: dont, lequel, auquel
la préface, qui sera lue…
le livre que j’écris
replaces “de + …”
le manuscrit dont je vous ai parlé (parler DE)
place or time
le jour où elle est partie
after a preposition (avec, dans, pour, sur…)
la voix avec laquelle elle parlait
auquel / à laquelle
à + lequel
la phrase à laquelle tu tiens (tenir À)
de + lequel, after a compound preposition
le tilleul près duquel elle repose
For people, “qui” is preferred after a preposition: “la femme avec qui il parle”. “Lequel” is required for things: “le stylo avec lequel j’écris”.
A typical mistake: “le livre que je t’ai parlé” ✗ (calqued on “the book I told you”). The verb is “parler DE” → “le livre dont je t’ai parlé” ✓.
4. Ce qui, ce que, ce dont: highlighting
To highlight an idea at the start of the sentence, French uses “ce qui / ce que / ce dont…, c’est…”:
What I like is her simplicity. (plaire: subject → ce qui)
What I want is to keep her voice. (vouloir qqch → ce que)
What the preface needs is a formal style. (avoir besoin DE → ce dont)
What I’m thinking about is the title. (penser À → ce à quoi)
After “ce dont” and “ce à quoi”, the second part keeps the preposition: “c’est D’un style soutenu”, “c’est AU titre”.
5. Registers
The same thing is said differently depending on the situation. At B2 you need to recognise the three registers and write in the standard or formal register:
un ouvrage
C’est pas facile.
Ce n’est pas facile.
Cela n’est guère aisé.
T’as vu ça ?
Tu as vu ça ?
Avez-vous remarqué cela ?
J’en ai marre.
J’en ai assez.
Je suis las de cette situation.

Signs of the formal register: subject inversion, “cela” instead of “ça”, “ne… guère”, abstract vocabulary, nominalisations, the imperfect subjunctive in literature. Signs of the informal register: dropping “ne”, “ça”, “on” instead of “nous”, slang words.
In the exam (DELF B2), the formal letter and the essay require a standard to formal register. A single “c’est pas” or “ça” in an official letter will lower your mark.

It all started with a question from Simone Roux. It was the evening of the rubab, at the beginning of August 2037, after the rehearsal. The musicians were packing up their instruments, Farid was still holding his against his chest, and Simone, sitting on her chair with her stick between her knees, asked Isabelle, out of the blue: “Who will tell all this, when we’re gone?” Isabelle didn’t know what to answer. She said there was the film, the videos, the newspaper articles. Simone shook her head. She said films come and go, and videos get lost in phones. She was talking about something else. She was talking about a book.

Isabelle had been an editor for thirty years, at a big Paris publishing house. She had published hundreds of books, novels, essays, memoirs of famous people who couldn’t write and had to be rewritten from the first page to the last. In 1998 she had also turned down a manuscript that became a huge success with a competitor, something people in the trade still talked about. When she retired, she had promised herself never to touch a manuscript again. She used to say a retired editor was like a sailor ashore: he looks at the sea, but he no longer goes on board.

That night, though, she didn’t sleep. She sat in her mother’s armchair, in the flat on rue d’Austerlitz, looking at the big wardrobe in the hall. In that wardrobe, since 2031, was everything her parents had left behind and that she didn’t know what to do with. She had never had the courage to really open it. She sometimes opened it to take something out, the blue shawl for a concert, the score of the waltz for a recording, then closed it again very quickly, the way you close the door on a room that is too full. At five in the morning, Haruka found her asleep in the armchair, the key to the wardrobe in her hand.

On Sunday 6 September they took everything out. Haruka had pushed the living-room table against the window and spread a big white tablecloth over it. Isabelle began an inventory, in a school exercise book, with an editor’s precision. She wrote without verbs, the way lists are written: “Twenty-three logbooks of Henri’s, from 1962 to 1985, cloth covers, variable condition. Seven notebooks of Odile’s, notes on trees, recipes, addresses. One hundred and forty-two letters, ninety of them from Henri to Odile. One cassette, Dakar, 1978. One handwritten score of the waltz. One blue shawl. One dried lime blossom, 1962.” Haruka thought it read like a poem.

They spent the day reading. Odile’s notebooks were easy to read: a doctor’s handwriting, small and hurried but regular, and short, direct, often funny sentences. “The lime tree in the courtyard is thirsty. So am I.” “Madame Petit won’t take her pills. She says they’re too pretty to swallow.” “Henri’s back on Thursday. Buy bread, oranges and a new supply of patience.” Isabelle laughed and cried at the same time. She recognised her mother’s voice in every line, with the Marseille accent you could hear even in her writing. Haruka, for her part, noted in the margin every word she didn’t know. There were a lot of them.

Henri’s logbooks, on the other hand, were almost illegible. Henri wrote in pencil, often in the rain, on a moving boat, with sailors’ abbreviations that nobody understood any more. “Vt NO 6, mer forte, 2 ris, cap 210, quart 0-4, RAS.” Whole pages looked like that. Haruka asked if it was a secret code. Isabelle laughed and said yes, in a way: it was the secret code of sailors, and the last man who spoke it fluently, Yves Le Goff, had died a year earlier. They looked at the twenty-three logbooks piled on the white tablecloth. They would need help. A lot of help.

That evening Isabelle phoned Hortense Valmont and Julien. They came the following Wednesday. They talked about style, about Odile’s voice, about the preface, about the title. Hortense found some sentences too informal for a book. Julien defended every word of Odile’s as if he were defending Odile herself. By the end of the evening they agreed on three things. The book would be called “Leave your door open”. The preface would be written by Hortense, in the formal style she was a master of. And the book would be published on 3 May 2038, the day of the lime trees, which was also Hélène’s birthday and the day she died.

The news spread faster than expected. A week later, Isabelle received a letter from Paris, on thick paper with a gold letterhead. It came from Éditions Saint-Clair, one of the biggest publishing houses in the capital, and it was signed by Valère Dumontel, the editorial director, a former colleague of Isabelle’s whom she didn’t much like. The letter was written in an impeccable administrative style. Isabelle read it aloud that evening to Haruka, putting on a deep, slightly ridiculous voice and underlining every word with her index finger, like a schoolteacher marking a particularly bad dictation.

“Dear Isabelle, further to the circulation of information regarding the preparation of a work devoted to your mother, and in view of the renown acquired by the story of the Thursday orchestras, I am pleased to offer you the publication of the said work in our main list. An advance of forty thousand euros could be paid to you upon signature of the contract. The rewriting of the text would be entrusted to an experienced author, in order to guarantee smooth reading and optimal distribution.” Isabelle put the letter down. She said: “Did you notice? Four sentences, and not a single living person in them.”

The next day, Valère Dumontel phoned. He was more direct than on paper. He explained that an old lady’s notes and a sailor’s logbooks wouldn’t sell. What was needed was a novel. A real novel, with a love story, a bit of jealousy, perhaps a rival in Dakar, and a happy ending. He even had a title: “The Sailor’s Waltz”. He added that the author he had in mind had already written three bestsellers on similar subjects and knew how to “make old papers sexy”. Isabelle listened politely to the end. Then she said: “Valère, what this book needs isn’t money. It’s the truth.” And she hung up.

One problem remained, and it wasn’t a small one. Without a big publishing house, you had to do everything yourself: layout, proofreading, printing, distribution. And you needed money. Amina opened a spreadsheet, of course. She calculated that printing two thousand copies, on good paper with a hardback cover, would cost nine thousand four hundred euros. She suggested a subscription: each reader would pay for their book in advance, twenty euros, and receive it on 3 May. They only needed four hundred and seventy subscribers to cover the costs. Isabelle thought that was a lot. Amina said there were forty-three orchestras in the network.

The subscription opened on 1 October. Every Saturday Bernard Delorme set up at the Croix-Rousse market with a little folding table, a handwritten sign and his trumpet, on which he played three notes each time a new subscriber signed. The op-ed club subscribed as a block, six copies each, “one for oneself and five to convert the ignorant”. Monique got her whole choir to sign. In Brest, Lille and Grenoble, the Thursday orchestras passed the sheet round during rehearsals. After three weeks there were one thousand six hundred subscribers. Amina had to enlarge her spreadsheet twice.

Now Henri’s logbooks had to be deciphered. During the All Saints’ holidays, Isabelle, Haruka, Julien and Rose-Hélène took the train to Le Croisic, with the twenty-three logbooks in a suitcase that nobody but Isabelle was allowed to carry. Nathalie, Yves’s daughter, was waiting for them on the station platform, in a yellow oilskin, in a fine drizzle. She still lived in her father’s stone house on the harbour. She had been a nurse in Brest for thirty years, but she had grown up on boats, and she read sailors’ abbreviations the way other people read the morning paper.

They worked for four days in Nathalie’s kitchen, in front of the window overlooking the harbour. Nathalie read aloud, translating. “North-westerly wind force six, rough sea, two reefs in the mainsail, heading two hundred and ten, midnight-to-four watch, nothing to report.” Haruka typed everything into her computer. Julien checked the dates. Rose-Hélène, who was nine and a half and couldn’t sit still, was in charge of finding on a big nautical chart every port where Henri had stopped. She marked them with red drawing pins. By the end of the week, the chart looked like a sky full of red stars.

On the third day, Nathalie stopped in the middle of a page. She went pale. Then she smiled. In the 1978 logbook, for two weeks, the handwriting changed. It was no longer Henri’s. It was bigger, more slanted handwriting, with cheerful spelling mistakes. Nathalie recognised it at once: it was her father’s. Henri had had a high fever off Dakar, and Yves had kept the logbook in his place. On the last day, Yves had written at the bottom of the page: “Henri is better. He played the harmonica tonight. Badly. So he really is better.” Nathalie asked if she could photograph the page. Isabelle gave her the whole page.

On the fourth day, it was Isabelle who stopped. She was reading the 1970 logbook herself, because Nathalie had gone out to buy bread. She was looking for a particular date: 12 February 1970, the day she was born. Henri was at sea, she knew that. Her mother had always told her he had heard the news by radio, three days later, off the coast of Africa. She found the page. There were the usual abbreviations, the wind, the sea, the heading. And underneath, in handwriting more careful than usual, as if for once Henri had wanted to write neatly, there were four lines that nobody had ever read.

“15 February. Radio message from Marseille. A girl, born on the 12th. Isabelle. Three kilos two hundred. I’m three thousand miles away, off Dakar, and I can’t give her anything. Odile says she screamed very loudly. Good. She’ll know how to answer.” Isabelle reread the four lines ten times. Then she put the logbook down, went out into the wind and walked to the end of the jetty, in the rain, without a coat. Julien followed her at a distance, without coming close. She stood facing the sea for a long time. When she came back, her hair was soaked and her eyes were red, and she said only: “He knew. From the very first day, he knew.”

On the last day, Loïc, the fisherman who had taken Yves out to sea on his last voyage, offered to take them out on the Marie-Jeanne. The sea was calm, grey and silver. Isabelle brought the 1985 logbook in a plastic bag. Out at sea, Loïc cut the engine, and Nathalie read aloud a page of Henri’s written almost in the same spot fifty-two years earlier: “Fair sea, light wind, gannets everywhere. Thought of Odile.” Rose-Hélène asked what a gannet was. Loïc pointed to a big white bird diving into the water like an arrow. Rose-Hélène said Henri had chosen his birds well. Nobody knew what she meant, but everyone felt it was true.

Back in Lyon, the real work began: proofreading. Isabelle decided that every page would be reread by at least three people and read aloud before being printed. She said a text that can’t be read aloud is a text that lies somewhere. The proofreading sessions took place on Thursday evenings, after the rehearsal, at Gérard’s café, which stayed open until midnight and served soup to everyone. It was called “the committee”. The committee was made up of whoever wanted to come, provided they could read and accepted being wrong at least once an evening.

The most formidable member of the committee was Monsieur Castaing, the retired Latin teacher from the op-ed club. He was eighty-four, with a terrifying memory and a passion for relative pronouns. He could argue for forty minutes about whether to write “le port dont il parlait” or “le port duquel il parlait”. He was always right, which was unbearable. The second most formidable member was Farid. He corrected nothing, but he read every page aloud, slowly, with his accent. Whenever he stumbled over a sentence, Isabelle rewrote it. She said: “If Farid understands, everyone will understand.”

Bertrand, for his part, had the opposite passion to Monsieur Castaing’s: he adored the passive. He had spent forty years writing reports in which nobody ever did anything, but in which everything “was decided”, “was noted” or “was brought to the attention of”. He suggested transforming Odile’s sentences accordingly. “Henri’s back on Thursday” became, under his pen, “Henri’s return is scheduled for Thursday”. The committee laughed, but Bertrand wasn’t discouraged. One evening, to teach him a lesson, Gérard put up a slate above the counter on which he had written: “The soup has been prepared by the owner. It will be served to those by whom it will have been ordered.” Bertrand found the sentence perfect. Everyone else ordered a beer.

There were terrible debates. The longest was about a sentence of Odile’s written in 1987: “This morning the upstairs neighbour drove me up the wall (m’a escagassée) with his drill.” Hortense wanted to replace “escagassée” with “exaspérée”, which was correct and understandable to everyone. Julien refused. Monsieur Castaing pointed out that the verb came from Provençal and had its place in a book devoted to a woman from Marseille. Simone Roux said that, in any case, “exaspérée” didn’t mean the same thing, because you could be exasperated politely, whereas you couldn’t be escagassée politely. The committee voted. “Escagassée” stayed, nineteen votes to one.

There were also evenings when nobody argued. One Thursday in November, Farid was reading aloud a page Odile had written in 1992. In it she talked about a patient, a young man from Kosovo who had crossed Europe on foot and didn’t speak a word of French. He had come to her surgery with a terrible fever. Odile had written: “I don’t understand what he says. He doesn’t understand what I say. We understood each other anyway. I’ll have to teach him the word ‘tomorrow’.” Farid stopped. He reread the last sentence more slowly. Then he put the sheet down and went out to smoke on the pavement, although he didn’t smoke. When he came back, he said only: “For me, it was Inès who taught me ‘tomorrow’.”

So that readers would understand all the same, Haruka suggested a glossary at the end of the book. She was the best person to do it: from the very first day she had noted in the margin every word a foreigner couldn’t understand. There were Odile’s Marseille words, “fada”, “peuchère”, “s’escagasser”, Henri’s sailor’s words, “ris”, “quart”, “amure”, and a few Lyon words that Parisians didn’t know. Rose-Hélène had suggested footnotes. Hortense had explained to her what they were. Rose-Hélène had said footnotes were “little words that look at the text from underneath”, and that she found that rude.

Meanwhile, Hortense was battling with the preface. She had written thousands of articles in forty years of journalism, editorials, columns, op-eds that had brought down a minister. But she couldn’t manage this preface. She started it over eleven times. The first version was twelve pages long and quoted Montaigne, Hugo and Camus. The fifth was only two pages, but it was written entirely in the passive, like a Court of Audit report, which Bertrand found admirable and everyone else found icy. The eighth was so short and dry that Monsieur Castaing asked whether it was a telegram.

One evening in December, Hortense came to see Julien on rue d’Austerlitz, the eleventh version in her hand, discouraged. She asked him what was wrong. Julien read the preface. It was perfect, elegant, without a single mistake, with impeccable nominalisations and relative pronouns Monsieur Castaing would have been proud of. Julien said: “It’s very beautiful. But I can’t hear you. I hear a journalist. Odile wouldn’t have asked you to be brilliant. She would have asked you to answer.” Hortense was silent for a long time. Then she took a blank sheet and wrote, without stopping, for an hour.

The twelfth version was a page and a half long. It quoted nobody. It began with a very simple sentence: “My mother learnt to read at thirty.” In it Hortense told the story of Jeanne Valmont, the seamstress from Place Sathonay, who had hidden for thirty years that she couldn’t read, and who had learnt at night with her daughter’s books. She told how Odile Bernard, whom she had never met, had taught her, at seventy, something as difficult as reading: to be quiet and listen. The last sentence said: “This book is a door. It is open. Come in without knocking.” The committee listened in silence. Nobody corrected anything.

At Christmas the book began to travel before it even existed. Ioana had translated about twenty pages into Romanian, the ones where Odile talked about lime trees, for Grandma, who was ninety-one, and for Viorica, who was ninety-seven. She had sent them to Iași and Bucharest in a big envelope. Grandma answered by phone that she had read everything twice, with her glasses and a magnifying glass, and that Odile was right about lime trees: you have to talk to them. Viorica answered with a three-page letter, in French, in shaky but perfect handwriting, to demand an original copy. She said you don’t read a translated voice, you listen to it from afar.

Haruka, for her part, was translating for her grandmother in Kyoto. She went slowly, one page an evening, and she got stuck for three days on a single word: “Answer”. In Japanese there were two ways of writing the verb “to answer”, pronounced exactly the same. The first meant answering a question, as in an exam. The second meant answering a call, a feeling, someone who is waiting for you. Haruka explained this to the committee one Thursday evening, drawing the two characters on a paper napkin. Monsieur Castaing said French was a poor language. Haruka chose the second character.

Her grandmother replied in January, with a postcard of Kyoto’s Silver Pavilion under snow. She had written five lines in French, like the first time, with the help of Aoi and a dictionary. “Haruka. I read the pages. This lady Odile, she is like me. She listens more than she talks. On 3 May, I come.” Haruka thought she had misunderstood. Her grandmother was eighty-four. She had never left Japan. She was afraid of planes. Haruka called her that same evening. Her grandmother confirmed, very calmly, that Aoi had already bought the tickets, and that at her age, being afraid of planes was a waste of time.

In January the cover had to be chosen. The printer had suggested hiring a professional graphic designer, a talented young man who worked for several Paris publishers. The designer sent three proposals. They were very beautiful. The first showed the sea at sunset, with the title in gold letters. The second showed an old photo of Henri in sailor’s clothes, retouched in black and white. The third showed a musical score flying away. The committee looked at them for a long time, politely. Then Isabelle said what everyone was thinking without daring to say it: they were beautiful, but they looked like covers for a different book.

That was when Rose-Hélène took a drawing out of her school bag. She had done it in class, secretly, during a geography lesson. It was a door, a plain wooden door, ajar, painted blue. Through the opening came a yellow light that spread across the floor. Behind the door you could make out the branches of a lime tree. And at the top of the drawing, above the door, there were five parallel lines, like a musical stave, on which she had drawn eight empty boxes. Nobody needed to ask what it was. Simone Roux took out her handkerchief. Monsieur Castaing declared it was the best cover he had seen since 1962.

Isabelle didn’t want to decide alone, because she thought it unfair to compare a nine-year-old’s drawing with a professional’s work. So they held a vote. The four proposals were displayed at Gérard’s café for a week, without names. The customers, the orchestra’s musicians and the children at Rose-Hélène’s school voted. The drawing of the blue door got two hundred and twelve votes out of two hundred and forty. The designer, when he was told the result, reacted gracefully. He asked if he could at least take care of the title’s typography, free of charge, so as to have his name somewhere next to Rose-Hélène’s.

On 4 March 2038, Rose-Hélène turned ten. For her birthday, Isabelle gave her the first printed proof of the cover, framed, with a line at the bottom in small letters: “Cover: Rose-Hélène Moreau-Popescu, aged ten. Typography: Thomas Lacroix.” Rose-Hélène looked at it for a long time without saying anything, which was rare. Then she asked if “aged ten” could be removed, because it sounded babyish. Isabelle said no, because in forty years’ time, when she was a great artist, it would be the only proof that she had started early. Rose-Hélène thought about it and found the argument admissible. She hung the frame above her bed, next to Henri’s harmonica.

For the printing, Isabelle had chosen the Rollet printing works, on the slopes of the Croix-Rousse, the last traditional printer in the district. In the sixteenth century, Lyon had been one of the printing capitals of Europe. Hundreds of thousands of books had been printed there, in Latin, French and Greek, in the workshops of rue Mercière, by the Saône. Almost nothing was left of that era, apart from a museum and a few stubborn craftsmen. Monsieur Rollet was one of them. He was eighty-one, with hands stained with ink for sixty-five years, and a granddaughter, Léa, who ran the business with modern machines and a great deal of patience.

Monsieur Rollet insisted on setting the title by hand, in lead type, as in Gutenberg’s day. He invited Haruka and Rose-Hélène to his workshop to show them. He took the little metal letters one by one from a big wooden type case, with tweezers, and lined them up in a composing stick. The letters were back to front; you had to read them as in a mirror. Rose-Hélène thought it was brilliant. Haruka thought it was very Japanese. Monsieur Rollet explained that the expression “être sous presse” (to be in press) came from this, and that in the old days, in this very workshop, the workers sang to keep the rhythm of the press.

The book had taken its final shape. Isabelle had divided it into three parts. The first was called “The Sea”: Henri’s logbooks, selected and translated from sailors’ language by Nathalie, with Rose-Hélène’s chart of red stars. The second was called “The Land”: Odile’s notebooks, her notes on trees, her patients, her neighbours, her recipes and her outbursts. The third was called “The Silence”: the letters, and the testimonies of those who had answered. At the beginning there was Hortense’s preface. At the end, Haruka’s glossary. And between the parts, a blank page, with nothing on it, which the printer didn’t understand.

The testimonies had raised an unexpected problem of style. Isabelle had asked each of the forty-three orchestras to send a page. She had received seventy. There was everything. A letter from Brest, written by an old sailor, in French mixed with Breton words. A page from Marseille, in Vieux-Port French, with a “peuchère” on every line. A page from Clermont-Ferrand written by sixty-three children, one sentence each. A page by Bertrand, in administrative style, with numbered paragraphs. Hortense had suggested harmonising everything. Isabelle had refused. She had said: “Each voice in its own register. This book speaks all the languages of French.”

The hardest case was Sami’s. He had sent the text of his slam, “Eight Bars”, the one he had performed in front of three thousand people on Place des Terreaux, with its four voices: the La Duchère boy in verlan, Odile in plain French, the sailor in Marseille slang and the prefect in formal French. The committee was divided. Monsieur Castaing felt verlan had no place in a book. Inès felt that was exactly why it should go in. In the end, Sami himself found the solution. He suggested writing, on the right-hand page, a translation of his text into standard French. Monsieur Castaing said that was the method of bilingual editions of Virgil, and voted in favour.

Inès, for her part, had been put in charge of the back cover, the short text printed on the back of the book that has to make you want to buy it in a hundred and twenty words. She thought it would be easy. She had won a national public-speaking contest at fourteen and was now studying law. It took her three weeks. She discovered that a short text is much harder than a long one, because you can’t hide the useless words. Her final version began with a series of noun phrases, like a newspaper headline: “Twenty-three logbooks. Seven doctor’s notebooks. One waltz. Eight bars of silence. And forty-three orchestras that answered.”

On 1 April, a fortnight before the printing, Isabelle made a discovery that was no joke. Rereading the twenty-third logbook one last time, the one from 1985, she realised the last page was missing. It had been torn out, cleanly, along the binding. The logbook stopped in the middle of a sentence, on 14 June 1985, off Brest: “Tomorrow, last watch. Then…” Then, nothing. And yet it was Henri’s last voyage, the one after which he had come ashore for good. The book was supposed to end on that page. Without it, the first part ended on a word left hanging in the void.

Isabelle searched everywhere. In the wardrobe, in the drawers, between the pages of the other logbooks, in the boxes of letters, in the pockets of Henri’s old pea coat still hanging in the hall cupboard. Haruka helped her until two in the morning. Nothing. The next day, in desperation, she phoned Nathalie in Le Croisic. She didn’t really know why. Perhaps because in 1985 it was Yves who sailed with Henri. Nathalie listened. Then she said she would look in her father’s sea chest, in the attic, which she hadn’t yet had the courage to open since his death. She called back that same evening. Her voice was trembling.

In the chest, under the oilskins and the nautical charts, was Yves’s last logbook, the one from 2036, which ended with the words everyone knew: “End of my watch. Relief assured.” And slipped into the cover of that logbook, folded in four, yellowed, was a page torn out of another logbook, in pencil handwriting that Nathalie had learnt to recognise during the All Saints’ holidays. On the back of the page, Yves had written, in his big slanting hand: “To be given back to Isabelle, when the time comes.” Yves had kept it for fifty-one years. He had waited. Perhaps he didn’t know when the moment would be. Perhaps he had forgotten.

Nathalie didn’t want to trust the page to the post. She took the first morning train, with the page in an envelope, the envelope in a book and the book against her chest, and arrived in Lyon on 13 April, the day before the printing. Isabelle was waiting for her on the platform at Part-Dieu station. They sat down on a bench, among the hurrying travellers, and Isabelle unfolded the page. She read it once, in silence. Then she read it aloud, for Nathalie, who already knew it by heart, and for an old man sitting next to them, waiting for his train, who pretended not to listen.

“15 June 1985. Light wind, fair sea. Last watch. I’m coming ashore. Twenty-three years at sea, and I never learnt how to say goodbye to a boat. Odile is waiting for me. Isabelle too, who is fifteen and doesn’t know me well enough. I have everything to learn: to stay, to listen, not to leave when things get difficult. Odile says it’s harder than a storm. She’s right, as always. I’m leaving this logbook to Yves. Relief assured.” Isabelle folded the page again. Nathalie said that now she understood where her father’s last sentence came from. He hadn’t invented it. He had copied it, fifty-one years later, to answer his friend.

The page was added to the book overnight, in facsimile, at the end of the first part. Léa Rollet redid the layout until three in the morning. On 14 April, at nine o’clock, everyone was at the printing works on the slopes of the Croix-Rousse: Isabelle, Nathalie, Haruka, Julien, Ioana, the children, who had been allowed to miss school, Hortense, Inès, Sami, Amina, Farid and Simone, the whole committee and the op-ed club. The workshop smelled of ink and warm paper. The big modern press was waiting, with its rollers and indicator lights. Monsieur Rollet wore a grey overall and a tie, as if for a wedding.

Monsieur Rollet made a short speech. He said he had printed thousands of books in his life, directories, catalogues, theses, poetry collections nobody read and even, in 1979, the menu for a famous footballer’s wedding. But he said it was the first time so many people had come to watch a press start up. Then he asked who was going to press the button. Everyone looked at Isabelle. Isabelle looked at Rose-Hélène. Rose-Hélène stepped forward, very serious, with her blue ribbon and her three keys round her neck. She pressed the big green button. The press began to turn with the noise of a train.

The first sheets came out, covered in text, still warm. Then the covers, with the blue door and the yellow light and the eight empty boxes above. Rose-Hélène wanted to touch the ink of her door and was gently told off by Léa. At noon, the first bound copy came out of the machine. Monsieur Rollet picked it up with his ink-stained hands. He explained that, according to the tradition of the house, the first copy went to the author. But the author was no longer there. So he held the book out to Isabelle. Isabelle opened it and breathed in the smell of the paper, for a long time, with her eyes closed. Then she crossed the workshop and gave it to Simone Roux.

“You’re the one who asked the question,” said Isabelle. “In August. Who will tell all this, when we’re gone. Here is the answer.” Simone took the book on her knees. She opened it at the first page, where there was the dedication Isabelle had written and that nobody had read yet, not even the committee. Simone read it aloud, in her dance-band singer’s voice, a little cracked: “To my mother, who left her door open. To my father, who learnt to stay. To Yves, who kept the page. And to all those who, one Thursday evening, heard a silence and answered.” In the workshop, the press kept turning. Nobody else spoke.

Then they had to wait for the binding, three days during which Isabelle hardly slept. She used the time to write, by hand, a letter to each of the people who had worked on the book. There were fifty-three of them. To Monsieur Castaing she wrote that she had never met a proofreader so unbearable and so indispensable. To Bertrand, that she forgave him all his passives. To Farid, that he was the best reader she had had in thirty years in the trade. To Nathalie she wrote just one line: “Relief assured.” And to Monsieur Rollet she sent a bottle of Côtes-du-Rhône with a label she had composed herself, by hand, in back-to-front letters.

The two thousand copies were delivered on 22 April to rue d’Austerlitz, in eighty boxes. They were everywhere: in the hall, in the corridor, under the living-room table and even in the bath, which Isabelle had declared out of service until further notice. Isabelle’s two cats, who had come with her from Paris, immediately each chose a box to sleep in. Haruka, practising her scales in the middle of this paper fortress, said she felt as if she lived in a library. Gérard had turned the back room of his café into a dispatch centre. Every evening after work, the committee came to make up parcels.

There were one thousand eight hundred and forty subscribers. Bernard Delorme and his van took care of Lyon. Farid and Simone took care of Villeurbanne, by tram, with a shopping trolley that Simone pushed like a walking frame, which, she said, gave her exercise without looking like it. The forty-three parcels for the orchestras went by post, each with a short note from Isabelle. Amina ticked off each delivery in her spreadsheet, in green. Monsieur Castaing checked the addresses, because he trusted nobody with the spelling of town names. He found three mistakes, one of them in “Montpellier”, which made him happy for a week.

On 25 April the phone rang. It was Valère Dumontel, from Éditions Saint-Clair. Someone had sent him a copy. He had read it in one night, which hadn’t happened to him in years. He no longer talked about a novel, or rewriting, or making old papers sexy. He wanted to buy the rights for a paperback edition, with a big print run, in every bookshop in France. Isabelle let him talk. Then she set a single condition: not a comma would be changed. Not a Marseille word, not a sailor’s abbreviation, not a sentence of verlan, not an empty box on the cover. There was a long silence at the other end of the line. Then Valère Dumontel said: “Not a comma. Agreed.”

News arrived from everywhere. Viorica announced that she would take the night train with Ilinca and Professor Petrescu and would arrive on 1 May, “if God and the Romanian railways allow”. Haruka’s grandmother would land in Lyon on 2 May, accompanied by Aoi, after sixteen hours of travel and a stopover in Helsinki, of which she said she would remember nothing because she intended to sleep. Nathalie was staying in Lyon until the 3rd. And Lyon city hall had confirmed that on 3 May at eleven o’clock, the garden in La Duchère park would officially bear the name of Odile Bernard. The plaque was already in place, under a white sheet.

On 29 April, Hortense Valmont published a full-page article about the book in Le Progrès. For once she had written it without a single nominalisation in the headline. The headline simply said: “They answered”. The article told the story of the subscription, the Thursday committee, the page found in a sailor’s chest and the cover drawn by a ten-year-old. It ended with the address of the La Duchère garden and the time of the inauguration. The next morning, Gérard received forty calls from people who wanted to buy the book. He told them all he wasn’t a bookseller, but he could offer them a coffee while they waited for the paperback. Twelve came to drink it.

On the evening of 30 April, Isabelle took a copy of the book and went up to La Duchère alone, by bus, as her mother used to. It was mild. The park was almost empty. In the garden, the lime tree had new leaves, of such a tender green that it looked transparent under the streetlights. The plaque, under its white sheet, looked like a polite ghost waiting its turn. Isabelle sat down on the bench facing the tree, in the exact spot where her mother used to sit to talk to the lime trees. She opened the book at the second part, “The Land”, and read aloud the first sentence of Odile’s first notebook.

“Lyon, October 1986. New town, new neighbours, new trees. Nobody knows me. Good: I’ll be able to listen.” Isabelle smiled. She was about to read the next sentence when she heard, behind her, three notes on a harmonica. She didn’t turn round. She knew. Rose-Hélène sat down next to her on the bench, with her jacket that was too big, her blue ribbon and her three keys. She said she had come to water the lime tree, because it hadn’t rained for four days, and that she had seen a light. She had a small bottle of water in her hand that wouldn’t have been enough to water a houseplant. Isabelle pretended to believe her.

Rose-Hélène looked at the book. She asked if she could read the last page right away, just the last one, to find out how it ended. Isabelle gently closed the book and said no. She said the ending was for 3 May, in front of everyone, and that some endings had to be waited for. Rose-Hélène sighed, the way ten-year-olds sigh when they are refused something reasonable. Then she said, more quietly, that she too was waiting for an ending. She still had, in her desk drawer, the letter Odile had left her in 2031, with on the envelope: “For Rose-Hélène. For later.” She had never opened it.

“When is later?” asked Rose-Hélène. She had already asked her parents, Haruka, Simone and Monsieur Castaing, who had given her a twenty-minute lesson on the adverb “tard” without giving her an answer. Isabelle looked at the lime tree. She thought of her mother, who always chose her words with care, even the smallest ones. She said: “You’ll know. My mother never said ‘later’ at random. When the time comes, you’ll know without anyone telling you.” Rose-Hélène thought about it. She decided it was a grown-up’s answer, that is, an answer that wasn’t one, but she kept it all the same.

They stayed on the bench a little longer, without talking, watching the lime leaves move in the light of the streetlamps. Then Rose-Hélène emptied her little bottle of water at the foot of the tree, very solemnly, as if it were a ceremony. She whistled the first three notes of the waltz, softly, for the lime tree. And somewhere in the big tower block on the other side of the park, behind a lit window on the eighth floor, someone they didn’t know whistled the next three. Isabelle took Rose-Hélène’s hand. They walked down together to the bus stop. In three days, the door would open for everyone.

Reading text: A city council decision

French administrative texts make heavy use of nominalisation and the passive. Here is the decision by which the city of Lyon names the garden in La Duchère park. Underline the noun phrases and the passive verbs. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Délibération du conseil municipal
Subject: naming of the garden located in La Duchère park, near the Jeanne-Valmont media library. Rapporteur: Monsieur Bernard Delorme, city councillor.

Statement of reasons. The garden in question was laid out in 2029 on the initiative of the residents of the district. A lime tree was planted there, at the foot of which part of the ashes of Madame Odile Bernard were scattered in 2031, in accordance with her wishes.

Madame Bernard, a retired doctor, was behind a network of neighbourhood orchestras which today numbers forty-three ensembles throughout France. The waltz into which she introduced a silence of eight bars is now played every Thursday by several thousand amateur musicians.

Considering the residents’ attachment to this place, considering the petition signed by one thousand two hundred and fourteen people, and considering the favourable opinion of the culture committee, it is proposed to the city council that this place be named “Jardin Odile-Bernard”.

Decision. After deliberation, the city council adopts the proposal unanimously. The inauguration of the garden will take place on 3 May 2038, on the occasion of the publication of the work devoted to Madame Bernard. A plaque will be installed at the entrance to the garden.

Text of the plaque, chosen by the residents: “Jardin Odile-Bernard (1950-2031). Doctor, neighbour, musician of silence. Leave your door open.” This text was preferred to a more official version, judged too cold by the children of the district.
